nameStory: Despite its name, Jerusalem oak has no connection to Jerusalem or oak trees! The name likely comes from its deeply divided, oak-like leaves and perhaps its Mediterranean origins in the 'Holy Land' region. It's also called 'sticky goosefoot' for its glandular, tacky texture that will literally stick to your fingers.
description: Jerusalem oak is an annual herb that grows 1-3 feet tall with a distinctive sticky, almost greasy feel to all its parts. The plant has deeply cut, feathery leaves that give it an almost fern-like appearance, and it produces small clusters of tiny greenish flowers along its branched stems. This Mediterranean native has found its way to disturbed soils across New England, though it remains quite uncommon in our region.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, feathery leaves that look almost fern-like or resembling white oak leaves, with multiple lobes and a distinctly sticky, glandular surface that feels tacky to touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish flowers arranged in dense, branched clusters along the stems, each flower barely noticeable individually but forming distinctive feathery spikes

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual herb growing 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems that often have a reddish tinge, especially toward the base

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant feels sticky and glandular to touch, with a distinctive aromatic smell when crushed that's somewhat sweet and medicinal

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round seeds that form after flowering, often covered in the same sticky glandular hairs as the rest of the plant

habitat: Jerusalem oak thrives in disturbed soils, waste places, and along roadsides where the ground has been churned up. Look for it in sandy or gravelly soils, vacant lots, construction sites, and the edges of agricultural fields. It prefers full sun and well-drained conditions.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants emerge, showing their characteristic feathery leaves early in the growing season.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and begin flowering, with the distinctive sticky texture most pronounced during warm, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowers mature into seeds and plants begin to yellow and dry out, though the sticky leaves remain a good identification feature until frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Jerusalem oak is so sticky that small insects can actually get trapped on its glandular leaves and stems, making it function somewhat like a carnivorous plant even though it doesn't actively digest its victims!
confusionNotes: The deeply divided leaves might remind you of ragweed or some ferns, but Jerusalem oak's sticky, glandular texture is unmistakable once you touch it. Remember: if it feels tacky and smells aromatic when touched, you've found your Jerusalem oak.
contextualKnowledge: This plant was once classified in the genus Ambrosia (ragweeds) and even called 'Ambrosia mexicana,' which explains some older field guide confusion. Despite common names suggesting oak or geranium connections, it's actually in the amaranth family alongside spinach and quinoa.
compareHints: Jerusalem oak stands out from its Dysphania relatives by its deeply cut, almost fern-like leaves - Mexican tea and clammy goosefoot have much simpler, less divided leaves. The sticky, glandular texture is shared with some relatives, but none have quite the same feathery leaf appearance that gives Jerusalem oak its distinctive 'feathered geranium' nickname.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives like Mexican tea and Jerusalem oak, clammy goosefoot is much smaller and has the distinctive sticky texture.
Mexican tea differs from its relatives like clammy goosefoot and Jerusalem oak primarily by its much stronger, more pungent smell and its narrow, lance-shaped leaves.

Unlike its Dysphania relatives like Mexican tea (which has a strong, pungent odor when crushed) or clammy goosefoot (which feels sticky), winged pigweed is distinguished by its papery stem wings and lack of strong scent.
